title: Deep learning: training correctness
summary: Eight real PyTorch CPU exercises: uneven microbatches, padded losses, frozen normalization, inference state, checkpoint ownership, shifted targets, weighted gradient reduction and LoRA merging. Tensor code runs in the app; no GPU or cluster is claimed.

lessons.title: Weight uneven microbatches by sample count
lessons.body:
# Weight uneven microbatches by sample count

Accumulating the mean loss of every microbatch and then averaging microbatches gives a short final batch too much influence. To reproduce one full-batch mean gradient, sum each batch loss and divide by the total number of samples before backpropagation.

This exercise uses actual PyTorch autograd with a scalar parameter and deliberately unequal microbatches. It compares the gradient with the analytical full-dataset result. Distributed training has the same weighting question when local batch sizes differ. The local calculation does not execute an all-reduce or measure a real cluster.

```python
import torch
w=torch.tensor(0.,requires_grad=True)
x=torch.tensor([1.,2.])
y=torch.tensor([2.,4.])
loss=((w*x-y)**2).mean()
loss.backward()
print(w.grad.item())
```

## Review the design

This reproduces full-batch gradients for a decomposable squared loss. Batch-dependent layers, stochastic operations and optimizer steps between microbatches can break equivalence even when the arithmetic weighting is correct.
lessons.task: Implement accumulated_gradient(batches,w0), where each batch is (xs,ys) nonempty equal lists. Use one scalar torch parameter, squared loss summed per batch divided by total sample count, backward each batch and return the gradient as float. Reject no batches or invalid lengths.

checks.name: uneven batches equal full batch weighting
checks.code: assert abs(accumulated_gradient([([1,2],[2,4]),([3],[6])],0)+56/3)<1e-5

checks.name: partition does not change the gradient
checks.code: a=accumulated_gradient([([1,2,3],[2,4,6])],1);b=accumulated_gradient([([1],[2]),([2,3],[4,6])],1);assert abs(a-b)<1e-5

checks.name: invalid microbatches fail

lessons.title: Normalize sequence loss by valid tokens
lessons.body:
# Normalize sequence loss by valid tokens

Padded sequence positions should not train the model, and their count should not dilute the reported loss. Mask them before normalization and divide by the number of valid targets. An all-padding batch needs an explicit finite result with a valid zero-gradient connection.

The exercise uses real log-softmax and gather operations over logits. It checks both forward values and backward gradients. Token masking is separate from attention masking: one controls which targets contribute to the objective, while the other controls which context positions can influence predictions. A correct loss mask cannot repair future-token leakage in attention.

```python
import torch
logits=torch.tensor([[0.,0.],[0.,0.]])
logp=torch.nn.functional.log_softmax(logits,dim=-1)
print(-logp[0,1].item())
```

## Review the design

Masking and normalization define the optimization objective. Counting padded tokens in the denominator silently changes the effective learning rate as sequence lengths change between batches.
lessons.task: Implement masked_ce(logits,targets,pad=-1), logits shape [N,C], targets [N]. Mean negative log probability over non-pad targets only. Return logits.sum()*0 for all padding so backward works. Valid non-pad targets are class indices.
lessons.solution:
import torch
def masked_ce(logits,targets,pad=-1):
    mask=targets!=pad
    if not bool(mask.any()):return logits.sum()*0
    safe=targets.clone();safe[~mask]=0
    logp=torch.nn.functional.log_softmax(logits,dim=-1)
    losses=-logp.gather(1,safe.reshape(-1,1)).reshape(-1)
    return losses[mask].mean()

checks.name: padding does not dilute valid loss
checks.code:
import torch,math
x=torch.zeros(3,2,requires_grad=True);y=torch.tensor([1,-1,-1]);loss=masked_ce(x,y);assert abs(loss.item()-math.log(2))<1e-6

checks.name: padding has zero gradient
checks.code:
import torch
x=torch.zeros(2,2,requires_grad=True);masked_ce(x,torch.tensor([1,-1])).backward();assert torch.allclose(x.grad[1],torch.zeros(2));assert x.grad[0].abs().sum().item()>0

checks.name: all padding remains differentiable
checks.code:
import torch
x=torch.ones(2,3,requires_grad=True);loss=masked_ce(x,torch.tensor([-1,-1]));assert loss.item()==0;loss.backward();assert torch.allclose(x.grad,torch.zeros_like(x))

hints: Use a boolean target mask and safe indices for padded rows.
Normalize selected losses only; an empty selection needs an explicit zero loss.

lessons.title: Freeze parameters and running statistics separately
lessons.body:
# Freeze parameters and running statistics separately

Setting requires_grad to false freezes parameter gradients, but a normalization layer can still update running statistics in training mode. Calling train on the enclosing model recursively changes its children, so the backbone must be placed back in evaluation mode after the global mode change.

This exercise uses a real BatchNorm layer and verifies that a forward pass leaves its running mean unchanged. The new head stays trainable. Fine-tuning policies should separately state which parameters receive gradients, which modules update state and which stochastic layers remain active. One flag does not express all three choices.

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
body=nn.BatchNorm1d(2)
body.eval()
before=body.running_mean.clone()
body(torch.tensor([[1.,2.],[3.,4.]]))
print(torch.equal(before,body.running_mean))
```

## Review the design

Evaluation mode and gradient recording are independent. A frozen backbone may still need gradients with respect to its inputs in some tasks, so disabling parameter gradients is different from wrapping the whole computation in no_grad.
lessons.task: Implement prepare_finetune(model,backbone). Set model.train(), disable gradients for every backbone parameter, then backbone.eval(). Return the list of model parameters still requiring gradients.

checks.name: head remains trainable and backbone is frozen
checks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
b=nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2,2),nn.BatchNorm1d(2));h=nn.Linear(2,1);m=nn.Sequential(b,h);params=prepare_finetune(m,b);assert len(params)==2;assert all(not p.requires_grad for p in b.parameters());assert all(p.requires_grad for p in h.parameters())

checks.name: normalization statistics do not drift
checks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
b=nn.BatchNorm1d(2);m=nn.Sequential(b,nn.Linear(2,1));prepare_finetune(m,b);old=b.running_mean.clone();m(torch.tensor([[2.,3.],[4.,5.]]));assert torch.equal(old,b.running_mean)

checks.name: mode ordering is explicit
checks.code:
from torch import nn
b=nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1,1));m=nn.Sequential(b,nn.Linear(1,1));m.eval();prepare_finetune(m,b);assert m.training and not b.training and m[1].training

Filter the optimizer parameter list after setting requires_grad.

lessons.title: Restore module modes after a prediction helper
lessons.body:
# Restore module modes after a prediction helper

A shared evaluation helper should not permanently alter a caller's training policy. Save each module's training flag before switching to evaluation mode, perform prediction without gradient recording and restore the original flags even on failure.

Saving only the root flag is insufficient when a model intentionally mixes a training head with an evaluation backbone. This exercise preserves that mixed state and returns a detached clone so later mutations do not alias the prediction result. It does not make concurrent training and inference on the same mutable model safe; separate ownership is still required.

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
model=nn.Linear(2,1)
with torch.no_grad():
    result=model(torch.ones(1,2))
print(result.requires_grad)
```

## Review the design

Temporary mode changes are shared mutable state. This helper is correct for exclusive ownership; concurrent requests should use a stable inference model or synchronization rather than racing mode toggles.
lessons.task: Implement owned_prediction(model,x): save every module training flag, eval the model, return model(x).detach().clone() under torch.no_grad, then restore every saved flag in finally.
lessons.solution:
import torch
def owned_prediction(model,x):
    states=[(module,module.training) for module in model.modules()]
    try:
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():return model(x).detach().clone()
    finally:
        for module,training in states:module.training=training

checks.name: inference disables dropout and gradients
checks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
m=nn.Dropout(.5);m.train();out=owned_prediction(m,torch.ones(4,requires_grad=True));assert torch.equal(out,torch.ones(4));assert not out.requires_grad;assert m.training

checks.name: mixed module modes are preserved
checks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
m=nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1,1),nn.Dropout(.2));m.train();m[0].eval();owned_prediction(m,torch.ones(1,1));assert m.training and not m[0].training and m[1].training

checks.name: failures still restore caller state
checks.code:
def _bad(call, error=ValueError):
    try: call()
    except error: return True
    return False
import torch
from torch import nn
m=nn.Linear(2,1);m.train();assert _bad(lambda:owned_prediction(m,torch.ones(1,3)),RuntimeError);assert m.training

hints: Snapshot each module mode instead of only model.training.
Restore modes in finally and detach the returned tensor.

lessons.title: Capture a checkpoint that cannot drift with live weights
lessons.body:
# Capture a checkpoint that cannot drift with live weights

A state dictionary contains tensor references, not a frozen historical snapshot. Continuing training or mutating a parameter can therefore change an alleged best checkpoint in memory. Copy tensor state when capturing the checkpoint, and keep training progress metadata tied to that capture.

The exercise records actual model and optimizer state with a deep copy. It tests aliasing by modifying the live model after capture. Persisting and resuming a whole experiment additionally needs RNG, sampler, preprocessing and data-version state. A model-only snapshot is enough for inference recovery but not exact training continuation.

```python
import copy,torch
from torch import nn
model=nn.Linear(1,1)
snapshot=copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
with torch.no_grad():model.weight.fill_(9)
print(torch.equal(snapshot["weight"],model.weight))
```

## Review the design

Checkpoint completeness depends on the recovery goal. Exact continuation also needs randomness, sampling position and input pipeline state; this exercise proves ownership of the captured model, optimizer and step fields only.
lessons.task: Implement capture_training(model,optimizer,step) returning a deep-copied dict model=model.state_dict(), optimizer=optimizer.state_dict(), step=step. Later live tensor or optimizer-state mutation must not change the snapshot.

checks.name: weights are owned by snapshot
checks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
m=nn.Linear(1,1);o=torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(),lr=.1);s=capture_training(m,o,2);old=s['model']['weight'].clone();
with torch.no_grad():m.weight.add_(10)
assert torch.equal(s['model']['weight'],old);assert s['step']==2

checks.name: optimizer configuration is copied
checks.code:
from torch import nn
import torch
m=nn.Linear(1,1);o=torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(),lr=.1);s=capture_training(m,o,3);o.param_groups[0]['lr']=.9;assert s['optimizer']['param_groups'][0]['lr']==.1

checks.name: snapshot restores the prior model
checks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
m=nn.Linear(1,1);o=torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(),lr=.1);x=torch.ones(1,1);expected=m(x).detach().clone();s=capture_training(m,o,0)
with torch.no_grad():m.weight.add_(2)
m.load_state_dict(s['model']);assert torch.allclose(m(x),expected)

hints: Copy the combined checkpoint structure, not just its outer dictionary.
state_dict tensor values still refer to live state until copied.

lessons.title: Shift language-model targets instead of predicting the present
lessons.body:
# Shift language-model targets instead of predicting the present

A next-token objective pairs the logits at position t with the token at position t+1. Scoring a position against its own input can produce a deceptively easy task and a misleading loss. The final input position has no next token in the provided sequence and must be excluded.

This exercise computes actual cross-entropy on shifted tensors. It leaves attention construction outside the contract: a correct target shift is still invalid if the model's attention can see future tokens. Sequence packing also needs boundary masks so an unrelated document is not silently treated as the continuation of another.

```python
import torch
ids=torch.tensor([[2,4,1]])
print(ids[:,:-1])
print(ids[:,1:])
```

## Review the design

Target alignment, causal attention and document-boundary masking are separate correctness conditions. Passing this loss check establishes alignment, not that a complete language-model training pipeline is leak-free.
lessons.task: Implement next_token_loss(logits,tokens), logits [B,T,C], tokens [B,T], T>=2. Score logits[:,:-1] against tokens[:,1:] with mean cross entropy. Reject T<2.

checks.name: last position logits do not affect the objective
checks.code:
import torch
x=torch.zeros(1,3,2);t=torch.tensor([[0,1,0]]);a=next_token_loss(x,t);x[:,2,:]=torch.tensor([99.,-99.]);assert abs(next_token_loss(x,t).item()-a.item())<1e-6

checks.name: next rather than current token is the target
checks.code:
import torch
x=torch.tensor([[[0.,10.],[10.,0.],[0.,0.]]]);t=torch.tensor([[0,1,0]]);assert next_token_loss(x,t).item()<.001

checks.name: uniform loss and too-short input

lessons.title: Combine local mean gradients by their sample counts
lessons.body:
# Combine local mean gradients by their sample counts

Averaging worker mean gradients gives equal weight to workers, not examples. If workers processed different numbers of examples, the global mean gradient is a count-weighted reduction. This matters for short final batches and uneven work assignment.

The exercise performs the reduction on real local tensors and compares it with known weighted results. It is an algebraic prerequisite for distributed training, not an execution of DDP, an all-reduce backend or a multi-GPU benchmark. Real clusters additionally need consistent collective ordering, failure handling, synchronization and checkpoint recovery.

```python
import torch
gradients=[torch.tensor([2.]),torch.tensor([8.])]
counts=[3,1]
print(sum(g*n for g,n in zip(gradients,counts))/sum(counts))
```

## Review the design

A reduction formula does not establish a distributed execution guarantee. The declared local objective, token/sample denominators and collective scaling must agree before this weighting matches the intended global gradient.
lessons.task: Implement weighted_gradient(gradients,counts) returning sum(g*n)/sum(n), same-shaped tensors with positive integer counts. Reject empty/mismatched inputs, invalid counts and unequal tensor shapes. Do not modify the inputs.

checks.name: unequal counts change the mean
checks.code:
import torch
a=torch.tensor([2.,4.]);b=torch.tensor([8.,0.]);assert torch.allclose(weighted_gradient([a,b],[3,1]),torch.tensor([3.5,3.]))

checks.name: does not mutate local gradients
checks.code:
import torch
a=torch.tensor([2.]);b=torch.tensor([8.]);weighted_gradient([a,b],[1,1]);assert a.item()==2 and b.item()==8

checks.name: shape and count mismatches fail

hints: Weight each local mean by the number of examples that produced it.
Allocate a new result rather than accumulating in place into an input gradient.

lessons.title: Merge a low-rank adapter without changing its function
lessons.body:
# Merge a low-rank adapter without changing its function

A LoRA adapter represents a low-rank update as B times A, scaled by alpha divided by rank. Merging that update into a base weight should produce the same linear output as applying the base and adapter branches separately. Matrix orientation and scaling errors can silently spoil a fine-tuned model.

This exercise uses actual PyTorch matrix multiplication and checks functional equivalence. It does not perform quantization or optimize memory on a GPU. Merging a quantized base, changing dtype or repeatedly applying the same adapter introduces additional numerical and lifecycle decisions that require separate verification.

```python
import torch
base=torch.zeros(2,3)
a=torch.ones(1,3)
b=torch.tensor([[1.],[2.]])
print((base+b@a).shape)
```

## Review the design

Functional equivalence is the core merge contract. Artifact versioning must record whether an adapter has already been merged, because merging the same update twice changes the model again.
lessons.task: Implement merge_lora(base,a,b,alpha) for base [out,in], a [rank,in], b [out,rank]. Return a new tensor base+(alpha/rank)*(b@a); reject nonmatrix inputs, incompatible shapes or rank<1; do not modify any input.
lessons.starter:
def merge_lora(base, a, b, alpha):
    return None

checks.name: merged and branched functions agree
checks.code:
import torch
w=torch.tensor([[1.,2.],[3.,4.]]);a=torch.tensor([[2.,1.]]);b=torch.tensor([[1.],[2.]]);x=torch.tensor([[3.,4.]]);m=merge_lora(w,a,b,2);assert torch.allclose(x@m.T,x@w.T+2*(x@a.T)@b.T)

checks.name: rank scaling and input ownership
checks.code:
import torch
w=torch.zeros(2,2);a=torch.eye(2);b=torch.eye(2);m=merge_lora(w,a,b,2);assert torch.equal(m,torch.eye(2));assert torch.equal(w,torch.zeros(2,2))

checks.name: invalid rank and shape fail

Scale by alpha/rank exactly once and return an out-of-place sum.
